page.text:
Limits and continuity capture the rigorous mathematical essence of
continuous change, geometric proximity, and local approximation.

Formulated in the mid-nineteenth century by Karl Weierstrass, the
$\epsilon$-$\delta$ definition dispenses with nebulous infinitesimals in
favor of precise universal and existential quantifiers: a function $f$
approaches $L$ at $x_0$ if for every tolerance $\epsilon > 0$ demanded in
the output, there exists a response radius $\delta > 0$ in the input
ensuring $|f(x) - L| < \epsilon$.

Continuity at a point means that $f(x) \to f(x_0)$ as $x \to x_0$.
Globally, continuous functions preserve the fundamental topological
invariants of subsets: the continuous image of a connected set is
connected (yielding the Intermediate Value Theorem), and the continuous
image of a compact set is compact (yielding the Extreme Value Theorem and
uniform continuity).
